docs.title: Chapter 3 — The Construction and Exhaustion of the Old Stability Regime
docs.text:
Japan’s post-bubble stability was not an illusion. It was an institutional achievement built from policies and balance sheets that prevented a damaged banking system, a deflationary economy, and a rapidly expanding public debt from producing disorder at the same time. The state replaced private demand when firms and households repaired their finances. Banks were recapitalized and nonperforming loans were gradually resolved. The Bank of Japan drove short- and long-term rates toward zero, supplied abundant liquidity, and eventually removed a large share of government-bond duration from the market. Domestic institutions recycled private financial surpluses into public liabilities. Corporate caution weakened growth but strengthened balance sheets. Japan’s external assets generated income and reduced dependence on foreign-currency finance.

The same structure imposed costs. Adjustment was slow. Weak firms and low-return assets remained in place. Wage and price growth became inert. Bank profitability was compressed. The JGB market lost depth as the Bank of Japan’s holdings increased. Fiscal policy expanded without creating a durable primary surplus. Household savers received little return on safe assets. These were not side effects outside the regime. They were part of the price paid for continuity.

For most of the period, the trade was sustainable because the costs reinforced the stabilizers. Corporate caution reduced borrowing demand and inflation. Low inflation allowed low nominal rates. Low rates reduced debt service. A large domestic saving-investment surplus supplied funding. A strong external asset position insulated the currency from the external rollover risks faced by high-debt emerging markets. Political incrementalism distributed losses over time rather than forcing one sector to absorb them at once.

The regime is now weakening because its components no longer point in the same direction. The behavior that suppressed wages and prices has begun to change. The Bank of Japan has left negative rates and yield-curve control. Marginal government borrowing costs are rising before the public balance sheet has been repaired. Demographic contraction is moving from a disinflationary influence into a labor- and service-capacity constraint. The yen and imported energy prices are transmitting external pressure into households and the budget. Political compensation is increasing when monetary normalization requires greater fiscal discipline.

The old regime did not fail on a single date. It is being consumed.

docs.title: 3.1 From balance-sheet crisis to managed adjustment
docs.text:
The first half of the 1990s destroyed the assumptions on which the late-bubble financial system had operated. Equity and land prices fell, collateral values deteriorated, and the banking system accumulated nonperforming loans. Firms entered a prolonged period of deleveraging and balance-sheet repair. The Asian financial crisis and Japan’s domestic banking failures in 1997 intensified caution. By the late 1990s, deflation was not simply a fall in the consumer-price index; it was the nominal expression of weak demand, impaired intermediation, debt reduction, and defensive corporate behavior.

The policy response was gradual. Authorities protected deposits and liquidity, recapitalized banks, expanded public credit, used fiscal stimulus, and eventually forced greater recognition of bad assets. This sequencing reduced the probability of a disorderly liquidation but prolonged the adjustment. Research on Japan’s post-crisis experience identifies delayed bank recapitalization and incomplete restructuring as major reasons the recovery remained weak.1 The delay was economically costly. It was also institutionally stabilizing in the narrow sense that credit losses were spread across time, the banking system remained intact, and mass foreclosure was avoided.

The resulting economy was not frozen. Export industries remained competitive, households retained large financial assets, corporations reduced leverage, and public infrastructure and social services continued to function. But the private sector’s objective changed. Firms that had experienced the destruction of collateral and the danger of debt prioritized liquidity, retained earnings, and financial independence. Banks facing weak borrowers and later compressed margins prioritized balance-sheet survival. Households facing uncertain employment and aging increased precautionary behavior.

The Bank of Japan’s retrospective review attributes part of the decline in Japan’s natural rate of interest to the cautious risk-taking behavior of firms after the bubble, lower potential growth, and demographic change. It also describes the eventual entrenchment of a norm in which wages and prices were assumed not to rise easily.2 That norm was not merely psychological. It was the repeated outcome of firms protecting volumes and employment by suppressing price increases, workers accepting limited nominal wage growth in exchange for employment stability, and policymakers supporting aggregate demand without forcing rapid resource reallocation.

The old stability regime therefore began as a response to private balance-sheet damage. It became a durable political economy after the immediate crisis had passed.

docs.title: 3.2 Deflation became a fiscal asset
docs.text:
Deflation is usually described as a burden on debtors because it raises the real value of nominal liabilities. That was true for Japanese firms and households during the early post-bubble adjustment. For the sovereign balance sheet, however, the subsequent low-inflation regime created a different effect. It allowed the government to issue and refinance debt at extraordinarily low nominal rates for a prolonged period.

Japan’s fiscal deficits did not disappear. Their carrying cost was suppressed. As short rates approached zero and the yield curve flattened, successive vintages of JGBs entered the debt stock at progressively lower coupons. The Ministry of Finance also lengthened the maturity structure. By the end of FY2025, the average remaining maturity of outstanding government bonds was roughly nine and a half years and the weighted-average interest rate was approximately 0.98 percent.3

That combination turned time into the government’s principal buffer. A long maturity schedule prevented market-rate changes from repricing the entire stock. Low coupons reduced the interest component of the annual budget even as gross debt increased. Each year of near-zero yields extended the period before the fiscal cost of the accumulated stock became visible.

The mechanism can be stated directly:

persistent low inflation → low policy and market rates → low coupons on new and refinanced JGBs → slow effective-rate transmission through long maturities → fiscal capacity to run deficits without an immediate interest shock.

This was not costless monetary financing. The Ministry of Finance still issued debt and investors still held claims on the state. Nor was it proof that the debt stock could grow without limit. It was a powerful intertemporal subsidy: the economic consequences of borrowing were deferred because the nominal price of time was exceptionally low.

The fiscal benefit helps explain why gross-debt warnings produced little immediate market response. Investors were not pricing the debt ratio in isolation. They were pricing a yen liability within a disinflationary economy, a domestic institutional system, a long maturity structure, and an increasingly active central bank. Under those conditions, the annual flow remained manageable even when the stock appeared extreme.

docs.title: 3.3 Domestic intermediation closed the funding circuit
docs.text:
The old JGB market was sustained by more than household patriotism or generic “home bias.” Japan’s financial architecture converted domestic savings into demand for government liabilities.

Households held deposits, insurance products, pension claims, and postal savings rather than building JGB portfolios directly. Banks, insurers, pension funds, and public financial institutions then allocated part of those funds into government securities. Banks required liquid, low-risk yen assets. Life insurers and pension funds required duration to match long-dated liabilities. The postal system and public institutions operated under mandates and portfolio structures that favored domestic fixed income. Regulatory and collateral frameworks increased the utility of JGBs throughout the system.

Hoshi and Ito described this closed funding circuit as a central explanation for the persistence of low JGB yields. Their warning was that an aging population and declining private saving could eventually weaken the capacity of domestic investors to absorb a growing public balance sheet.4 The timing of that adjustment proved slower than a simple household-saving model implied because the institutional investor base, corporate financial surpluses, and Bank of Japan purchases grew in importance.

Domestic ownership reduced run risk. A bank or insurer managing yen liabilities does not evaluate JGBs like a foreign leveraged fund evaluating an unhedged sovereign position. It has structural reasons to hold safe domestic assets and can accept lower yields than an investor demanding currency and political-risk compensation. A broad domestic base also allows the government to alter maturity, issuance composition, and distribution channels without depending on one external buyer class.

This did not eliminate price risk. It changed the form of adjustment. Domestic institutions could absorb more debt at low yields, but the cost appeared through low investment returns, compressed margins, duration exposure, and reduced portfolio flexibility. The state was less exposed to an abrupt foreign funding stop because households and institutions absorbed a continuing financial claim on future domestic income.

The funding circuit was therefore stabilizing at the level of the sovereign and distributive at the level of the economy. It placed part of the fiscal burden inside deposits, insurance returns, pension portfolios, and bank balance sheets rather than on an explicit annual tax bill.

docs.title: 3.4 The Bank of Japan became the market’s architect
docs.text:
The Bank of Japan’s role evolved in stages. It adopted the zero-interest-rate policy in 1999, quantitative easing in March 2001, comprehensive monetary easing in 2010, quantitative and qualitative monetary easing in April 2013, a negative policy rate in January 2016, and QQE with yield-curve control in September 2016.5

Each stage expanded the Bank’s influence over financial conditions. Early quantitative easing targeted the quantity of current-account balances. QQE greatly increased the scale and maturity of JGB purchases. Negative rates pushed the lower bound below zero. Yield-curve control moved from influencing the curve through purchases to publicly targeting the approximate level of the 10-year yield, backed by fixed-rate purchase operations and a large balance sheet.

The monetary objective was to escape deflation and achieve the 2 percent price-stability target. The fiscal effect was inseparable from the implementation. Large-scale purchases lowered the term premium, compressed yields across maturities, and removed duration from private portfolios. The government could issue debt into a market in which the central bank was continuously altering the supply-demand balance.

The Bank’s 2024 review concluded that unconventional easing had positive effects on economic activity and prices, although the effect on prices was smaller than originally expected because inflation expectations and wage-price behavior were difficult to change. It also found negative effects on JGB-market functioning and a contraction in bank lending margins, while noting no clear evidence at that point that financial intermediation had been impaired in aggregate.6

That balanced assessment is important. The BOJ did not merely “print money” to fund the state, and the program cannot be reduced to a failed inflation experiment. It lowered real and nominal financing costs, supported asset prices and credit, reduced the probability of deflationary contraction, and gave fiscal policy time. At the same time, its growing stock of JGBs reduced the amount available for private trading and altered yield formation.

Bank of Japan research on individual JGB issues finds a nonlinear relationship. Purchase flows can increase transaction volume by facilitating trades, but a large BOJ ownership share reduces circulating supply, widens bid-ask spreads after thresholds are crossed, and distorts the yield curve. Continuous fixed-rate operations reinforce that effect.7

The BOJ’s success therefore changed the nature of the market it was stabilizing. It prevented yields from becoming the clearing price of fiscal risk, but private price discovery weakened as a result. Once yield-curve control ended, the state did not return to the pre-QQE market. It entered normalization with the central bank still holding an enormous stock and private investors being asked to rebuild a marginal pricing role.

docs.title: 3.5 Corporate caution financed public continuity
docs.text:
The corporate sector’s post-bubble transformation was another stabilizer. Japanese firms moved from being major net borrowers toward persistent financial surplus. Deleveraging reduced vulnerability to interest rates and banking stress. Retained earnings and liquid assets provided a buffer against recession, supply shocks, and exchange-rate volatility. Large firms could maintain employment and investment through periods when domestic demand was weak.

The national accounting counterpart was equally important. A government deficit can be financed domestically when other sectors save more than they invest. Japan’s nonfinancial corporations became a major source of that surplus. In FY2024, nonfinancial corporations recorded net lending equivalent to approximately 2.2 percent of nominal GDP, while the general government remained a net borrower.8 Funds did not move from a corporate treasury directly into a ministry account, but the sectoral balance closed through banks, capital markets, insurers, pensions, and foreign asset transactions.

The corporate surplus reduced sovereign funding pressure while weakening the domestic growth mechanism. A firm retaining cash rather than investing or raising wages strengthens its own balance sheet and adds to national saving. It also reduces current household income and private capital formation. The same behavior that made the financial system safer helped entrench weak demand and low inflation.

This was one of the old regime’s most stable exchanges:

cautious firms → lower borrowing and wage pressure → greater private financial surplus → more funds available to financial intermediaries → easier absorption of public deficits → weaker domestic demand and continued need for public support.

The state substituted for demand that private firms did not generate, while the private surplus helped finance the substitution. The loop could persist at near-zero rates because the carrying cost of the public response remained low.

The aggregate strength also concealed heterogeneity. Large exporters accumulated cash and foreign income, while smaller domestically oriented firms operated with thinner margins and greater dependence on bank credit. The corporate buffer was national in accounting terms but uneven in its practical availability. Later chapters examine why that distinction matters once rates, wages, and import costs rise together.

docs.title: 3.6 External wealth insulated the regime
docs.text:
Japan’s external balance sheet distinguished it from conventional sovereign-debt crisis cases. Persistent current-account surpluses accumulated into a large net international investment position. By the end of 2025, Japan held 1,805.6 trillion yen of external assets against 1,243.9 trillion yen of liabilities, leaving a net position of 561.8 trillion yen.9

The composition of the current account also changed. As Japan’s manufacturing production and investment moved abroad and energy imports increased, primary income from direct and portfolio investment became a more important source of surplus than the trade balance. Bank of Japan balance-of-payments analysis identifies investment income as a major contributor to the current account since the latter half of the 2000s.10

This structure provided four stabilizers.

First, Japan did not need continuing foreign-currency borrowing to finance the state. Second, overseas income supported the current account even when the goods trade balance weakened. Third, yen depreciation increased the yen valuation of foreign assets and foreign-currency income. Fourth, Japanese institutions possessed external portfolios that could be rebalanced or repatriated under stress.

The buffer had limits that were easy to overlook. Most of the net external position was privately owned. Reinvested foreign earnings did not necessarily return as domestic wages or investment. Valuation gains caused by yen depreciation increased measured national wealth while the same depreciation reduced household purchasing power. The foreign asset position protected external solvency more effectively than it protected the median domestic consumer.

This distinction allowed macroeconomic stability and household compression to coexist. The nation could become wealthier in yen terms as the currency weakened, even while imported necessities became more expensive and domestic real income deteriorated.

docs.title: 3.7 Demography initially lowered the price of time
docs.text:
Japan’s aging population is now treated primarily as a fiscal burden. During the construction of the old regime, its monetary effects also supported stability.

Lower fertility and longer life expectancy reduced labor-force growth, weakened potential output, and encouraged saving for longer retirement. Firms facing weaker trend demand required less domestic capital. The resulting excess of desired saving over investment contributed to a lower natural rate of interest. Bank of Japan research estimates that demographic change accounted for about 270 basis points of the decline in Japan’s real interest rate between 1960 and 2015.11

The demographic effect was not linear. Women and older workers entered the labor force at higher rates, slowing the decline in employment even as the working-age population contracted. Japan’s 15–64 population was approximately 73.7 million in 2024, or 59.6 percent of the total, while participation gains among women and seniors offset part of the numerical decline.12 These gains expanded the usable labor pool without reversing the age structure.

For the old regime, demography therefore produced a temporary alignment:

  • weaker labor-force growth reduced potential growth and investment demand;
  • longer expected retirement supported precautionary saving;
  • lower natural rates made extraordinary public debt cheaper to carry;
  • rising participation delayed the point at which labor scarcity became fully binding;
  • low wage pressure reinforced the norm of weak price adjustment.

The same alignment stored future pressure. A larger elderly population increased pension, healthcare, and long-term-care claims. Higher participation could not be repeated indefinitely once the available pool of women and older workers narrowed. Retirees eventually shifted from accumulation toward asset decumulation. Rural depopulation raised the cost of maintaining services per resident.

Demography helped create the low-rate environment in which the public balance sheet expanded. It did not create the future revenue required to service that balance sheet once rates normalized.

docs.title: 3.8 Energy and the permissive external price regime
docs.text:
Japan has always been resource constrained, but the macroeconomic cost of that constraint varies with global prices, the exchange rate, and the domestic energy mix. For much of the old stability period, disinflation abroad, stable supply chains, and periods of yen strength limited the domestic price impact of import dependence. After the global financial crisis, weak international demand and then the 2014–2020 commodity-price environment further reduced the pressure.

The Fukushima disaster changed the structure by reducing nuclear generation and increasing reliance on imported fossil fuels. Subsequent reactor restarts and renewable investment improved the position, but energy self-sufficiency remained only 15.3 percent in FY2023, the lowest in the Group of Seven according to the 2025 Energy White Paper.13

Low domestic energy self-sufficiency was not a binding macro constraint when the yen and global fuel prices were favorable. It became one when both moved against Japan. The key transition was not a new physical dependence; it was the loss of a price environment that had allowed the dependence to remain politically manageable.

Energy exposes the difference between nominal and real sovereignty. Japan can create yen and issue JGBs to subsidize electricity, gas, gasoline, or kerosene. It cannot create the imported fuel being purchased. The subsidy changes which domestic balance sheet pays the higher external price. During the old regime, the need for that transfer was intermittent. In the emerging regime, weak-yen and geopolitical exposure make it recurrent.

docs.title: 3.9 Political incrementalism distributed the loss
docs.text:
Japan’s political system did not resolve the post-bubble adjustment through a single fiscal consolidation, banking purge, or labor-market rupture. It used repeated packages, administrative guidance, credit guarantees, transfers, public works, tax adjustments, and gradual institutional reform. Policies were often criticized as too small, too late, or internally inconsistent. Their cumulative function was to prevent concentrated losses from destabilizing the system.

Incrementalism matched the financial architecture. Long-maturity debt distributed fiscal cost across years. Relationship banking distributed corporate losses across loan renewals and restructurings. Lifetime-employment norms and bonus adjustment distributed labor cost without mass dismissal at large firms. Monetary easing distributed the sovereign cost across low asset returns and central-bank holdings. Supplementary budgets distributed shocks across future taxpayers and bondholders.

This was not uniquely Japanese risk aversion. It was a coherent method of maintaining social and institutional continuity in an economy with weak nominal growth. Its political advantage was that no single decision appeared to impose the full adjustment. Its economic disadvantage was that low-productivity structures, regional obligations, and temporary support could survive beyond their original justification.

The method worked best when delay was cheap. Near-zero rates made tomorrow’s fiscal cost appear small. Low inflation made nominal benefit levels and wages easier to hold. A stable currency limited the need for recurring household compensation. Once those conditions reversed, incrementalism became more expensive because every delay entered a higher-rate, higher-cost, and more distributionally contested future.

docs.title: 3.10 How the stabilizers reinforced one another
docs.text:
The old regime was durable because the buffers formed a circuit rather than a list.

Stabilizer Immediate function Reinforcing link Deferred cost Corporate deleveraging Reduced private default risk Created financial surplus Weak wages and domestic demand Household and institutional saving Funded banks, insurers, and pensions Supported JGB demand Low returns and future decumulation BOJ easing and JGB purchases Lowered rates and prevented deflation Reduced public and private financing costs Market-function and exit problems Long debt maturity Delayed budget repricing Allowed gradual issuance adjustment Higher costs accumulated with a lag Fiscal expansion Replaced weak private demand Preserved employment and income Larger debt stock and recurring programs External assets Generated income and reduced external risk Supported current account and yen balance sheet Income weakly transmitted to households Low inflation norm Stabilized nominal contracts Allowed ultra-low rates Wage inertia and low price flexibility Political incrementalism Avoided concentrated loss Sustained institutional consent Deferred reform and embedded compensation

The circuit explains why forecasts based on one exhausted buffer repeatedly failed. A decline in household saving did not trigger a JGB crisis because corporate saving and BOJ purchases expanded. Weak trade balances did not trigger an external crisis because primary income remained strong. Rising gross debt did not trigger a debt-service shock because coupons fell and maturities lengthened. Poor bank margins did not stop intermediation because institutions changed business models, consolidated, and retained access to central-bank liquidity.

Japan’s resilience was adaptive. The system replaced one weakening stabilizer with another. The danger in the current regime is that several replacements are now being withdrawn or becoming costly at the same time.

docs.title: 3.11 The break in alignment
docs.text:
The first formal break came in prices. Large import shocks after 2021 pushed inflation above the ranges that had governed corporate and household behavior. Firms became more willing to pass costs forward. Labor scarcity strengthened wage demands. The Bank of Japan concluded in 2024 that the two-decade norm of wages and prices not rising was changing.14

The second break came in monetary structure. In March 2024, the BOJ declared that negative rates and yield-curve control had fulfilled their roles and returned the short-term rate to the center of policy. By June 2026, the rate had reached 1 percent. At its July meeting the Board held that level, but one member proposed 1.25 percent, while the Bank projected core inflation clearly above 2 percent from the second half of FY2026.15

The third break came in sovereign pricing. The effective rate on the debt stock remained low, but marginal JGB yields rose and BOJ purchases declined. Private investors were being asked to absorb more duration after years in which the central bank had dominated supply. The low-coupon inheritance still protected the budget, but it was no longer being renewed at the same price.

The fourth break came in the distribution of nominal growth. Higher prices and corporate earnings improved tax revenue and nominal GDP. Households simultaneously faced elevated food, energy, housing, and service costs. The government responded through subsidies, transfers, and proposed tax relief. Part of the fiscal gain from inflation was therefore committed to compensating for inflation.

The fifth break came in saving and capacity. The FY2024 household saving ratio was only 0.8 percent on the revised national-accounts basis, while nonfinancial corporations continued to run a financial surplus.16 The domestic funding circuit had not disappeared, but it depended less on a broad household surplus and more on institutions, corporate balances, and the BOJ. At the same time, labor-force participation gains were approaching practical limits and age-related service needs were rising.

None of these changes alone ends the regime. Together they reverse its internal logic.

Old alignment: low inflation supported low rates, low rates supported fiscal expansion, and private surpluses funded the state. Emerging alignment: inflation requires higher rates, higher rates reprice the state, and fiscal expansion is used to offset the inflation and credit effects of normalization.

The old system turned weak demand into cheap public finance. The new system turns nominal improvement into a conflict over who will absorb higher prices and yields.

docs.title: 3.12 What remains of the old regime
docs.text:
Exhaustion does not mean disappearance. Japan still possesses every major institutional defense that prevented a conventional crisis.

The debt remains overwhelmingly yen denominated. Average maturity is long. The Bank of Japan can alter purchase operations and provide liquidity. Domestic banks, insurers, and pensions retain structural demand for JGBs. The country remains a net external creditor. Corporate balance sheets are stronger than in the 1990s. The government can mobilize tax, regulatory, and administrative capacity. The financial system remains broadly resilient.

These facts make a sudden funding stop improbable as a base case. They also shape the form of future adjustment. Japan is more likely to respond to stress through renewed central-bank purchases, issuance changes, subsidies, tax measures, regulatory incentives, and gradual balance-sheet transfers than through explicit default or abrupt austerity.

The distinction between buffer and solution is therefore essential. A buffer reduces the probability of discontinuity. A solution restores the system’s capacity without creating an equivalent future claim. Long maturity is a buffer; it does not prevent higher coupons from entering over time. BOJ purchases are a buffer; they do not eliminate inflation or market-function costs. External assets are a buffer; they do not automatically fund the general account. Corporate cash is a buffer; it does not guarantee domestic investment or broad wage growth.

Japan still has buffers. The old regime is exhausted because those buffers are now being asked to absorb different pressures simultaneously.

docs.title: 3.13 Counterarguments and limits
docs.text:
Three counterarguments qualify the transition.

First, normalization could improve the regime rather than exhaust it. Positive rates can restore bank margins, improve market price discovery, reward household saving, and reduce resource misallocation. That is correct. The issue is sequencing. These long-run benefits arrive while the government refinances at higher coupons and weaker borrowers face immediate adjustment. Successful normalization requires the fiscal and private sectors to absorb the transition without forcing the BOJ back into suppression.

Second, stronger wage and price behavior may finally create the virtuous cycle the old regime failed to produce. A durable rise in real wages, consumption, productivity, and domestic investment would broaden the tax base and reduce dependence on fiscal demand. This is the principal successful-stabilization path. It is not established by nominal wage settlements alone. The gains must extend beyond large firms and exceed the price effects transmitted through food, energy, housing, taxes, and services.

Third, corporate and external wealth may replace declining household saving. Japan’s private sector remains wealthy and capable of holding public liabilities. The constraint is not a mechanical shortage of yen savings. It is the return required to mobilize those funds, their willingness to remain in domestic duration, and the distributional cost of using private wealth to support public borrowing rather than domestic consumption and investment.

These counterarguments reduce the probability of a hard break. They do not re-create the alignment of the zero-rate era.

docs.title: 3.14 Finding: Japan consumed the conditions that protected it
docs.text:
The old stability regime worked because several apparent weaknesses offset one another. Corporate caution suppressed investment but created financial surplus. Demographic aging reduced potential growth but lowered the natural rate. Deflation weakened nominal demand but allowed the state to finance itself cheaply. Domestic intermediation limited market discipline but prevented an external funding stop. BOJ purchases impaired price discovery but stabilized the sovereign curve. Political delay embedded costs but prevented concentrated adjustment.

Japan did not survive three decades by proving that debt, demography, or monetary limits were irrelevant. It survived by converting each constraint into a stabilizer for another part of the system.

That conversion is becoming harder. Inflation has changed corporate behavior. Monetary normalization is removing the rate subsidy. Higher marginal yields are entering a debt stock accumulated under different assumptions. Household relief is consuming fiscal gains. Labor scarcity and energy imports are imposing real constraints that nominal balance-sheet operations cannot erase.

The transition can be summarized as follows:

managed adjustment created low inflation → low inflation created low rates → low rates financed public substitution for weak private demand → BOJ purchases and private surpluses stabilized the expanding debt stock → the resulting debt and market structure made exit increasingly consequential → the return of inflation forced the exit before fiscal repair was complete.

Chapter 4 begins at that final step. It examines how the low-rate inheritance is consumed through refinancing and why the annual flow of debt service—not the gross-debt headline—is the first fiscal mechanism through which the old regime becomes a current constraint.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Fiscal Dominance and the Refinancing Constraint
docs.text:
Japan’s public debt is usually discussed as a stock: a ratio above 200 percent of gross domestic product, a central bank holding an extraordinary share of the sovereign-bond market, and a government that has operated with persistent deficits for most of the past three decades. Those facts describe the scale of the inherited balance sheet. They do not, by themselves, identify the constraint that matters most over the next decade.

The operative constraint is a flow. It is the annual cost of refinancing a large stock of low-coupon debt while the state continues to finance ordinary expenditure, demographic obligations, strategic investment, energy relief, disaster response, and political compensation. Japan does not have to refinance its entire debt stock at current yields in a single year. That is precisely why a sudden sovereign-funding crisis is the wrong baseline. The pressure arrives gradually, through the maturity schedule, and accumulates in the budget. Each year of higher marginal yields converts another portion of the low-rate inheritance into a higher permanent carrying cost.

This distinction changes the fiscal argument. Japan is not “running out of money” in the conventional sense. It issues debt in its own currency, possesses deep domestic financial institutions, holds large public and external assets, and retains a central bank capable of stabilizing market functioning. The relevant question is narrower and harder: how much of the government’s annual revenue can be absorbed by debt service and aging-related expenditure before other policy becomes structurally dependent on additional borrowing?

The answer cannot be read from the gross-debt ratio alone. It depends on five interacting variables: the primary balance, the effective interest rate on the outstanding debt, nominal growth, the maturity and holder structure of Japanese government bonds, and the political tendency to treat supplementary spending as an ordinary instrument of economic management. In the current regime, these variables are moving in the same direction. The average coupon remains low, but the marginal cost of financing has risen. Nominal growth has raised tax revenue, but it has also raised indexed expenditure and strengthened demands for relief from inflation. The debt ratio has declined, but interest costs are rising. The budget therefore looks healthier by one headline measure while becoming more exposed by another.

That is the fiscal core of slow compression.

docs.title: 4.1 The budget is larger than the initial budget
docs.text:
The FY2026 initial general-account budget totaled 122.3 trillion yen. Tax revenue was budgeted at 83.7 trillion yen, other revenue at 9.0 trillion yen, and new government-bond issuance at 29.6 trillion yen. On the expenditure side, social security accounted for 39.1 trillion yen, local allocation tax grants for 20.9 trillion yen, and national debt service for 31.3 trillion yen.1

These figures immediately establish two points. First, debt service and social security together absorb 70.3 trillion yen, equivalent to 84 percent of budgeted tax revenue. That comparison does not imply that particular taxes are legally earmarked to those two categories. It shows the scale of the government’s committed expenditure relative to its recurring tax base. After those two functions, only 13.4 trillion yen of budgeted tax revenue remains against more than 50 trillion yen of other general-account spending.

Second, the initial budget is not a reliable measure of the state’s actual annual fiscal posture. In June 2026, only two months into the fiscal year, the Diet received a 3.11 trillion yen supplementary budget responding to energy-price and Middle East risks. The entire amount was financed through additional special deficit-financing bonds. It raised the FY2026 general account to approximately 125.42 trillion yen.2 The government argued that market issuance would not increase because roughly 3 trillion yen of previously scheduled FY2025 bond issuance could be cancelled after stronger revenue and unspent appropriations were taken into account. That claim was mechanically plausible at the time. It did not change the economic character of the supplement: new FY2026 expenditure was matched by new FY2026 deficit-financing authority, while a prior-year issuance requirement happened to fall.

This form of intertemporal netting is important. It allows the government to say that a new package will not enlarge current market issuance even though the underlying fiscal commitment has increased. The debt market may be protected from an immediate supply shock, but the budget has still acquired new obligations. If the favorable prior-year adjustment is not repeated, the same policy in a later year requires additional issuance or a different offset.

The FY2025 supplementary budget illustrates the scale that can emerge. Its general-account framework totaled 18.3 trillion yen, including 17.7 trillion yen in additional spending; when related tax reductions and special-account measures were included, the government described the national package as 21.3 trillion yen.3 These numbers must not be added interchangeably. The 21.3 trillion yen figure was the broad policy package, not a 21.3 trillion yen increase in the general account. The relevant point is institutional: a package of this size was enacted after an initial budget of 115.2 trillion yen, making the supplementary process part of the effective annual fiscal baseline rather than an exceptional correction.

The distinction between the initial budget and the realized fiscal stance therefore needs to be formalized:

Initial budget + supplementary appropriations + tax expenditures and special-account measures = effective annual policy stance

Not every supplementary appropriation is wasteful, discretionary, or avoidable. Earthquakes, energy shocks, security contingencies, and recession can require rapid action. The problem is not the existence of a supplementary process. It is the migration of recurring policy into that process. Winter utility relief, gasoline support, SME assistance, wage subsidies, strategic-industry funds, and regional transfers repeatedly appear as urgent responses even when their underlying causes persist across fiscal years.

Once that happens, the initial budget understates the state’s structural call on resources. A nominal primary surplus calculated before the next package can coexist with an expansionary realized stance after it.

docs.title: 4.2 Debt service is not the same as interest expense
docs.text:
Japan’s FY2026 national debt-service appropriation of 31.3 trillion yen is often misread as an interest bill. It is not. The total includes 13.0 trillion yen of interest payments and related expenses, with the remainder principally representing transfers for debt redemption. The distinction matters because redemption transfers are largely financed within a system that issues refunding bonds under the 60-year redemption rule. They represent a real budgetary and debt-management flow, but they are not equivalent to the economic cost of interest.4

Three related measures should therefore be kept separate:

Measure FY2026 reference What it captures Interest payments ¥13.0T Current carrying cost in the general account National debt service ¥31.3T Interest plus redemption-related budget transfers Gross JGB issuance ¥180.7T New financing, refunding, and other issuance channels

The gross issuance figure is especially easy to misuse. The Ministry of Finance’s FY2026 plan called for 180.7 trillion yen of JGB issuance, of which 168.5 trillion yen was scheduled as market issuance on a calendar basis.5 Most of that amount did not represent an equivalent increase in net debt. Refunding bonds replace maturing obligations. Their issuance maintains the stock rather than financing 180.7 trillion yen of new expenditure.

This does not make gross issuance irrelevant. It identifies a different risk. Net borrowing measures the expansion of the debt stock; gross issuance measures the volume that must clear through the market. A country can reduce net borrowing while still facing a large refinancing requirement. For Japan, that requirement means investors must continually accept the rollover of an enormous inherited stock, and the price at which they do so progressively enters future budgets.

The Ministry of Finance estimated 1,145 trillion yen of outstanding government general bonds at the end of FY2026, or about 1,095 trillion yen excluding the authorized front-loading of refunding bonds.6 The stock had an average remaining maturity of roughly nine and a half years at the end of FY2025. Its weighted-average interest rate was still only 0.98 percent. That maturity structure is a buffer. It delays repricing. It does not prevent it.

The maturity schedule shows the front of the rollover wave. On the FY2026 initial-budget basis, approximately 158.0 trillion yen of general bonds mature in FY2027, 109.5 trillion yen in FY2028, 76.3 trillion yen in FY2029, and 79.7 trillion yen in FY2030.7 These figures are not forecasts of net issuance, but they show the amount of old financing that reaches a pricing event. When replacement coupons exceed the coupons of maturing debt, the effective interest rate on the stock rises even if the policy rate later stops increasing.

This is fiscal inheritance cannibalization. The low-coupon debt accumulated under zero and negative interest rates remains valuable, but each year of normalization consumes part of that inheritance. The deterioration appears gradual because the average rate moves far more slowly than current market yields. By the time the budget reflects the full effect, the higher coupons have already been locked into multiple vintages of bonds.

docs.title: 4.3 The Ministry of Finance already models the acceleration
docs.text:
The 2026 Debt Management Report provides a clearer basis for the debt-service path than broad claims about the debt ratio. Under the ministry’s 3 percent nominal-growth case, national debt service rises from 31.3 trillion yen in FY2026 to 34.7 trillion yen in FY2027, 38.0 trillion yen in FY2028, and 41.3 trillion yen in FY2029. Interest payments alone rise from 13.0 trillion yen to 21.6 trillion yen over the same period.8

Under its lower 1.5 percent nominal-growth case, national debt service reaches 40.3 trillion yen in FY2029 and interest payments reach 20.7 trillion yen. The slightly lower debt-service number in the weak-growth case is not evidence that weak growth is fiscally safer. It reflects the way tax revenue, local grants, borrowing needs, and assumed interest rates interact inside the ministry’s mechanical budget projection. The overall general-account deficit is worse in the lower-growth case.

The official sensitivity analysis is more revealing. If interest rates from FY2027 onward run one percentage point above the 3 percent-growth baseline, national debt service reaches 45.1 trillion yen in FY2029. At two percentage points above baseline, it reaches 48.9 trillion yen.9

Fiscal year MOF 3% nominal-growth case Rates +1 percentage point Rates +2 percentage points FY2026 ¥31.3T ¥31.3T ¥31.3T FY2027 ¥34.7T ¥35.5T ¥36.3T FY2028 ¥38.0T ¥40.1T ¥42.2T FY2029 ¥41.3T ¥45.1T ¥48.9T

This table resolves a central numerical question. A national debt-service cost near 50 trillion yen is not the Ministry of Finance’s baseline forecast. It is, however, almost exactly the ministry’s published FY2029 high-rate sensitivity. The stress estimate is therefore analytically legitimate when identified correctly:

Observed: FY2026 national debt service is 31.3 trillion yen. Official baseline: MOF projects 40.3–41.3 trillion yen in FY2029, depending on nominal growth. Official sensitivity: MOF reaches 48.9 trillion yen in FY2029 if rates are two percentage points above its baseline path. Monograph stress path: approximately 50 trillion yen around FY2029–FY2030 if high marginal yields persist and political spending is not durably offset.

The time lag matters. The FY2026 budget books an interest rate of 3 percent for the purpose of estimating debt-service costs, but that budgetary rate is not the same as the weighted-average coupon paid on the debt stock, the Bank of Japan’s policy rate, or the yield at any single maturity. It is an accounting assumption applied within the budget model. Market yields affect the realized cost as securities are issued and refinanced. A 10-year yield above the budget assumption does not immediately reprice the entire stock; it increases the cost of the bonds sold at that maturity and influences the broader curve.

The slow transmission can create false reassurance. The annual budget remains financeable, auctions continue to clear, and the effective rate stays below market rates. Yet the direction of travel has already been fixed for the debt vintages issued at higher coupons. Fiscal pressure is not absent during the lag. It is stored.

docs.title: 4.4 Why a falling debt ratio can coexist with a worsening fiscal position
docs.text:
Japan’s recent debt-ratio improvement is real, but its composition matters. Nominal GDP expanded rapidly as prices and wages rose, tax collections benefited from inflation and corporate profits, and the effective interest rate on the outstanding debt remained anchored by bonds issued during the low-rate era. The denominator grew faster than the average carrying cost of the numerator. That combination can reduce debt relative to GDP even while the nominal debt stock and annual interest expense continue to rise.

The standard debt-dynamics identity is useful:

\[ \Delta d_t \approx \frac{r_t-g_t}{1+g_t}d_{t-1}-pb_t \]

where \(d\) is the debt-to-GDP ratio, \(r\) the effective nominal interest rate, \(g\) nominal GDP growth, and \(pb\) the primary balance as a share of GDP. When nominal growth exceeds the effective interest rate, the “snowball effect” reduces the debt ratio. A primary deficit can then coexist with a falling ratio. When the relationship reverses, the same debt stock requires a primary surplus merely to prevent the ratio from rising.

At a debt ratio of roughly 188 percent of GDP, a seemingly small change in \(r-g\) has a large fiscal effect. If the effective interest rate exceeds nominal growth by half a percentage point, the government needs a primary surplus near 0.94 percent of GDP simply to stabilize the ratio. At a one-percentage-point gap, the stabilizing surplus approaches 1.88 percent of GDP. Using FY2026 nominal GDP around 689 trillion yen, those amounts are approximately 6.5 trillion and 13.0 trillion yen respectively. The calculation is deliberately approximate, but it establishes the scale of the exposure.

The Cabinet Office’s July 2026 projections make the same point through a more elaborate model. In its strongest growth-strategy case, the ratio of central and local government bonds to GDP falls from 187.6 percent in FY2026 to 170.6 percent in FY2040. In the second growth-strategy case it reaches 174.6 percent. In the current-trend case, however, the ratio bottoms near 180 percent around 2030 and then rises to 190.6 percent by FY2040. A lower-potential-growth sensitivity reaches 202.6 percent.10

Those ratios use the Cabinet Office’s central-and-local public-bonds measure, not the broader IMF measure of general-government gross debt. They should not be spliced together. Their value lies in the direction of the modeled path. Even the government’s current-trend case no longer produces a permanent decline. The ratio turns upward when primary-balance improvement weakens and the effective interest rate catches up.

The government’s favorable cases are also less reassuring than their ending debt ratios suggest. In the strongest growth case, the primary balance of central and local government reaches a surplus of 1.3 percent of GDP by FY2040, but net interest expense rises to 4.6 percent of GDP. The overall fiscal balance therefore remains in deficit and deteriorates to approximately 3.2 percent of GDP. In the second growth case, net interest expense reaches 4.4 percent of GDP and the overall deficit reaches roughly 3.4 percent.11

This is the central contradiction in “growing out of debt.” Faster nominal growth improves revenue and the denominator, but the growth strategy also assumes rising wages, prices, investment, and market rates. Over time, those rates enter the debt stock. The successful-growth cases do not eliminate the interest burden; they produce larger primary surpluses capable of partially offsetting it.

That distinction is frequently lost in political discussion. A falling debt ratio is treated as proof that fiscal space has been created. In the model, however, the ratio falls because several demanding assumptions hold simultaneously: real growth accelerates despite population decline, total factor productivity rises materially, labor participation improves, nominal growth remains firm, and primary surpluses persist even as aging and strategic expenditure continue. Failure in any one dimension does not cause an immediate crisis. It narrows the margin available in the others.

The International Monetary Fund’s 2026 assessment is directionally similar but less optimistic about the later path. It projected interest payments to rise by roughly 0.3 percent of GDP per year as debt is refinanced, doubling from 1.5 percent of GDP in 2025 by 2031 and exceeding 4 percent by 2036. The IMF baseline allowed favorable growth-interest dynamics to reduce gross debt through 2034, followed by an increase from 2035 as interest and age-related spending accumulated.12 The timing differs from the Cabinet Office’s current-trend case, but the mechanism is the same: a temporary window in which nominal growth outruns the effective rate does not guarantee a durable solution.

docs.title: 4.5 Supplementary budgets convert shocks into structure
docs.text:
The refinancing problem would be easier to manage if the primary budget adjusted automatically as interest costs rose. Japanese politics works in the opposite direction. The same inflation that raises nominal revenue reduces household purchasing power, increases procurement costs, raises social-security outlays, and creates pressure for tax relief and subsidies. Fiscal improvement on the revenue side generates demands for fiscal expansion on the expenditure side.

The June 2026 supplementary budget is a compact example. The government restored 513.5 billion yen to general contingency reserves after approving summer electricity and gas assistance, then created a separate 2.5 trillion yen reserve for Middle East and energy-related contingencies. The appropriation was not payment for energy already consumed. It was fiscal capacity reserved for a continuing shock.13 This was rational risk management in isolation. It also demonstrated that the initial budget did not contain enough durable room to absorb the policy consequences of energy dependence and a weak currency.

The deeper issue is recurrence. A subsidy that bridges a short, exogenous price spike can expire. A subsidy that compensates households for a structurally weak yen, recurring winter demand, and persistent import exposure becomes part of the political baseline. Withdrawal then produces a visible price increase even if the underlying wholesale price is unchanged. The state has not removed inflation; it has changed the payer and controlled the timing of recognition.

The consumption-tax proposal announced in July 2026 would intensify the same pattern. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the government intended to lower the tax rate on food from 8 percent to 1 percent for two years beginning in April 2027 and would seek non-debt financing through expenditure reform and non-tax revenue. At the July 31 evidence cutoff, the measure had been announced but not enacted, and its permanent financing had not been specified in legislation. Contemporary estimates placed the direct annual revenue loss near 4.4–5.0 trillion yen before related transfers.14

It would be analytically wrong to insert that full amount into the current budget as if the law were already in force. It would be equally wrong to leave it out of the forward fiscal risk. The July Cabinet Office model projected a 1.4 trillion yen central-and-local primary surplus for FY2027 after assuming 10 trillion yen of additional annual fiscal expenditure.15 A food-tax reduction of the reported size, without a durable offset, is several times larger than that projected surplus. The proposal therefore tests whether the official primary-balance path is a policy commitment or merely the residual of assumptions made before the next relief measure.

The proposed use of non-tax revenue does not settle the matter. One-off asset proceeds, fund surpluses, and foreign-exchange-account income can finance a temporary measure in a cash sense. They do not create a recurring tax base. If an annual tax reduction is financed by drawing down an asset or transferring an exceptional surplus, the first year may avoid additional bond issuance while the state’s balance sheet weakens. When the temporary resource is exhausted, the tax reduction must expire, another asset must be sold, expenditure must be cut, or borrowing must rise.

The temporary label is itself politically unstable. Restoring a consumption tax from 1 percent to 8 percent would create an abrupt and highly visible increase in food prices. The government may intend to restore the rate after two years, but households and firms will make decisions around the lower rate, and the restoration would approach the 2028 political cycle. The fiscal risk is not that the measure is certain to become permanent. It is that temporary relief creates a new constituency and a new reference price, raising the political cost of expiration.

This is how supplementary budgets and temporary tax measures narrow policy freedom without producing a conventional funding crisis. Each measure can be financed. The cumulative structure becomes harder to reverse.

docs.title: 4.6 Gross debt, net debt, and the asset argument
docs.text:
Japan’s large public asset position is a genuine counterweight to gross debt. The Ministry of Finance’s 2026 report placed general-government gross debt near 1,409 trillion yen and net debt near 537 trillion yen after subtracting roughly 872 trillion yen of financial assets, although the gross and net figures refer to defined statistical boundaries and market valuations.16 Any serious debt analysis must acknowledge this balance sheet.

The inference often drawn from it is too broad. Government assets reduce net indebtedness and generate income, but they are not fully interchangeable with tax revenue or liquid debt-service capacity. The portfolio includes assets with different owners, mandates, liquidity, currency exposure, and political constraints. Pension assets support pension obligations. Fiscal-loan assets are matched against financing functions. Foreign reserves support currency and external-liquidity policy. Equity stakes, infrastructure, and loans cannot all be liquidated rapidly without economic or political consequences.

An asset sale can reduce gross debt if the proceeds retire liabilities. It does not automatically improve net worth: an asset and a liability disappear together. If the same debt capacity is then used to finance current expenditure, the transaction has converted a financial asset into spending. That may be justified, especially if the spending creates a productive asset with a high return. It should not be described as free fiscal space.

Foreign-exchange reserves make the point sharply. Selling dollar assets to buy yen can reduce the reserve portfolio and, depending on the financing structure, allow associated financing bills to be retired. Gross public debt may decline. Net public debt changes little at the moment of exchange because both the foreign asset and the yen liability fall. If the government subsequently borrows to finance domestic spending, it has effectively exchanged part of its external asset buffer for a domestic fiscal program.

The relevant test is therefore not whether Japan owns assets. It is whether the income, liquidity, and institutional availability of those assets match the expenditure being justified. Recurring tax relief financed by nonrecurring asset conversion fails that test unless the policy also creates a durable offset.

docs.title: 4.7 Domestic funding remains powerful, but marginal pricing is changing
docs.text:
The claim that Japan’s debt is domestically funded remains partly true. It is no longer a complete description of the JGB market.

At the end of March 2026, the Bank of Japan held 42.2 percent of government bonds and treasury bills on a market-value basis. Depository institutions held 13.6 percent; insurers and pension funds, 16.4 percent; public pensions, 6.4 percent; households, 1.7 percent; and overseas investors, 13.7 percent.17 On the narrower measure excluding some categories and separating central-government securities, the BOJ share was higher. The exact percentage depends on the instrument boundary. The structural conclusion does not: the central bank remains the dominant holder, while private domestic institutions still own a large share.

Those holdings provide a formidable stability mechanism. Domestic banks need high-quality liquid assets. Insurers match long-duration liabilities. Pension funds maintain strategic allocations. The BOJ can alter purchase operations when market functioning deteriorates. These investors do not behave like a single leveraged foreign fund capable of abandoning the market in one trade.

The buffer nevertheless has limits. The BOJ is reducing purchases and allowing its holdings to decline as bonds mature. A BOJ board member stated in May 2026 that the Bank held about half of outstanding JGB issuance, that annual purchases had once exceeded 130 trillion yen, and that purchases were scheduled to fall below 30 trillion yen in FY2027 against annual government-security issuance near 180 trillion yen.18 The transition requires other buyers to absorb a larger marginal flow at yields they consider adequate.

Foreign investors are more important to that price-discovery process than their ownership share implies. At the end of December 2025 they held 12.8 percent of JGBs including treasury bills, but accounted for 47.2 percent of secondary-market spot transactions and 72.7 percent of futures trading.19 Their influence is concentrated in liquidity, hedging, relative-value trades, and the marginal price rather than long-term ownership alone.

This does not mean foreigners “control” the JGB market or that domestic absorption has disappeared. It means an auction can succeed at a materially higher yield and thereby validate a new funding cost. The government receives the money; the fiscal constraint still tightens. A high bid-to-cover ratio cannot erase that result if buyers demanded a larger concession.

The holder structure therefore supports the slow-compression thesis more than a crisis thesis. Japan retains enough institutional capacity to avoid disorder under most conditions. That same capacity permits higher costs to enter gradually, reducing the likelihood of a dramatic break while increasing the likelihood of prolonged budgetary adjustment.

docs.title: 4.8 Counterarguments and limits
docs.text:
Four counterarguments deserve direct treatment.

First, the Bank of Japan can suppress yields. It can. Renewed large-scale purchases, fixed-rate operations, or an explicit yield cap could interrupt a disorderly selloff. The cost is not technical inability but policy collision. Suppression while inflation remains above target can weaken the yen, increase imported inflation, enlarge the BOJ’s market footprint, and make the eventual exit more difficult. Yield control shifts the pressure; it does not remove it.

Second, inflation can reduce the debt burden. It can reduce the ratio while the effective rate remains below nominal growth. The benefit is strongest during the transition, when revenue and nominal GDP reprice faster than the inherited debt stock. It weakens as new coupons enter the stock and as spending responds to wages, prices, and household relief. Inflation is not fiscally useless. It is politically and temporally conditional.

Third, Japan has a current-account surplus and large net foreign assets. Those assets strengthen external solvency and reduce the risk of a classic foreign-currency crisis. They do not place the private sector’s foreign assets at the unrestricted disposal of the general account. Japan can remain externally wealthy while the government’s annual budget becomes more constrained.

Fourth, growth-oriented investment could raise productivity enough to stabilize the system. This is the strongest constructive counterargument. Productive public investment can raise potential growth, private capital formation, and tax revenue. The problem is not the possibility of a positive return. It is the burden of proof created by scale and timing. The return must be large enough, broad enough, and fast enough to exceed demographic drag, the cost of financing, and the tendency for temporary support to become structural. The Cabinet Office’s own scenario range shows how sensitive the debt path is to those assumptions.

These counterarguments weaken any prediction of imminent insolvency. They do not restore the policy freedom of the zero-rate era.

docs.title: 4.9 Finding: the constraint is fiscal oxygen
docs.text:
Japan’s fiscal position is best understood neither as an approaching bankruptcy nor as an unlimited sovereign-currency balance sheet. It is a system consuming inherited fiscal oxygen.

The inheritance consists of low coupons, long maturities, domestic institutional demand, BOJ holdings, public assets, and a period in which nominal growth exceeds the effective interest rate. These buffers remain large. They are also being used simultaneously. Higher marginal yields consume the low-coupon inheritance; repeated supplementary budgets consume revenue windfalls; tax relief consumes future tax capacity; reserve and asset arguments consume balance-sheet flexibility; and aging consumes an increasing share of primary expenditure.

The result is not a single fiscal cliff. It is a narrowing corridor:

higher yields → gradual refinancing at higher coupons → rising interest and debt-service flows → less room for ordinary policy → greater reliance on supplementary borrowing and one-off revenue → stronger market scrutiny of the next package → greater pressure on the Bank of Japan to contain yields.

That final step establishes fiscal dominance in the operational sense used throughout this monograph. The Bank of Japan remains legally independent and can still raise rates. The fiscal scale of its decisions nevertheless constrains the range over which monetary policy can move without activating debt-service, credit, banking, and political pressure.

Chapter 5 examines the other side of that constraint. The BOJ can defend inflation credibility and the currency by tightening, but tightening accelerates the refinancing mechanism described here. If it does not tighten, the yen becomes the pressure valve, importing the inflation that generates further fiscal relief. The monetary and fiscal boxes are therefore not parallel problems. They are one feedback system.
